title: Growing mustard microgreens
subtitle: The fastest and hottest brassica microgreen, ready to cut in 5 to 7 days
excerpt: Mustard microgreens are among the fastest brassica crops on a microgreen tray. The cotyledons develop in 5 to 7 days at room temperature and have a sharp, hot flavour that adds bite to salads and sandwiches.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

content.text: Mustard microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop. The cycle is 5 to 7 days from sowing to cut: sow densely on a 25 cm tray, blackout for two days, then move to light and cut with scissors when the cotyledons are fully expanded. The cotyledons are peppery and hot, noticeably sharper than radish at the same stage.
Mustard grows at a similar pace to radish, making the two natural tray companions. Sow them at the same time and cut them together for a mixed peppery microgreen blend.

Light source: a south or west-facing windowsill in spring and summer. In winter, a supplementary LED grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray for 14 to 16 hours a day gives more uniform growth. Mustard is slightly more tolerant of lower light than basil but produces better colour and texture under good light.
Ambient temperature: 18 to 22°C. Mustard germinates and grows readily at room temperature. Cold rooms slow the cycle; below 14°C germination is patchy.

Day 0: sow. Fill a 25 cm tray with pre-dampened seed compost or coir to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter mustard seed densely, 20 to 30 g per tray. Press gently into contact with the medium. Do not cover with soil.
Days 1 to 2: blackout. Stack a second tray on top, lightly weighted. Remove when shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall, which happens within 36 to 48 hours at room temperature.
Day 3 to cut: light and watering. Bring to light. Cotyledons green up within 24 hours.
only: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water and let the medium draw it up. Never pour water over the seedlings.

Days 5 to 7: cut. When cotyledons are fully expanded and standing 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium with sharp scissors. Rinse, spin dry, use fresh. Refrigerate in a sealed container for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting the tray
attrs.intro: Common problems with mustard microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Stems collapse and rot at the base
items.cause: Damping off from overwatering or poor airflow.
items.fix: Bottom-water only. Discard the affected tray and start fresh. Improve airflow around the tray for the next cycle.

items.cause: Top-watering or a cold damp room with no airflow.
items.fix: Switch to bottom-watering entirely. Run a small fan nearby. The mould is on the substrate, not the stems, and the cotyledons remain safe to cut.

items.cause: Seed distributed unevenly on the tray.
items.fix: Use a shaker motion from 20 to 30 cm above the tray to spread seed evenly. Avoid dumping from a packet directly onto the medium.

content.text: Use untreated mustard seed. White mustard (Sinapis alba) is the most common microgreen variety and the fastest. Brown mustard produces a more intensely hot cotyledon; red-stemmed mizuna-type mustards offer colour variation. All follow the same growing method.
risk is similar to radish. The short cycle means a failed tray costs little and the next one can go in immediately.
